'''uphasp''' (up-hȧsp′), ''v. t.'' To hasp or fasten up. ''Stanihurst'', Æneid, iv. 254. (''Davies.'') [Rare.]

'''uphaud''' (up-hâd′), ''v. t.'' A Scotch form of ''uphold.''

'''upheap''' (up-hēp′), ''v. t.'' To pile or heap up; accumulate. ''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 90.

'''upheaping†''' (up-hē′ping), ''n.'' [ME. ''upheping;'' < ''up'' + ''heaping.''] Accession; addition to full measure.
{{smaller block|The syngler ''uphepynge'' of thi welfulnesse.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 3.}}}}

'''upheaval''' (up-hē′val), ''n.'' The act of upheaving, or the state of being upheaved; a heaving or lifting up; specifically, in ''geol.'', a disturbance of a part of the earth’s crust, having as one of its results that certain areas occupy a higher position with reference to adjacent areas than they did before the disturbance took place.
{{smaller block|Upheaval is a part of the process by which mountain-chains have been formed; it is the opposite of subsidence. The subsidence of one region may cause the apparent upheaval of another adjacent to it.—'''Doctrine of violent upheavals.''' Same as ''theory of cataclysms'' (which see, under ''cataclysm'').}}

'''upheave''' (up-hēv′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''trans.'' To heave or lift up; raise up or aloft.
{{smaller block|Arcita anon his hand ''uphaf''.}}
readings.c1s2:
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1570.}}}}
{{smaller block|Continents are ''upheaved'' at the rate of a foot or two in a century. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 378.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be lifted up; rise.
{{smaller block|<poem>The pavement bursts, the earth ''upheaves''
Beneath the staggering town!</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Agnes.}}}}

¶
'''upheaving''' (up-hē′ving), ''n.'' The act or process of lifting up or being lifted up; an upheaval.
{{smaller block|All waves save those coming from submarine ''upheavings'' are caused by the wind. {{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LXII. 82.}}}}

'''upheld''' (up-held′). Preterit and past participle of ''uphold''.

'''uphelm''' (up-helm′), ''v. i.'' To put the helm to windward. ''Tribune Book of Sports'', p. 284.

'''upher''' (ū′fėr), ''n.'' In ''building'', a fir pole of from 4 to 7 inches diameter, and 20 to 40 feet long, sometimes roughly hewn, used in scaffoldings and sometimes in slight and common roofs, for which use it is split. ''Gwilt.'' [Eng.]

'''uphild†''' (up-hild′). An obsolete form of ''upheld'', preterit and past participle of ''uphold''. ''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. xi. 21.

'''uphill''' (up′hil′), ''adv.'' Upward; up, or as if up, an ascent: as, to walk ''uphill''.

'''uphill''' (up′hil), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Leading or going up a rising ground; sloping upward: as, an ''uphill'' road.—'''2.''' Attended with labor, fatigue, or exertion; difficult; severe; fatiguing; burdensome: as, ''uphill'' work; hence, not hav-

'''upholsterer-bee''' (up-hōl′stėr-ėr-bē), ''n.'' A bee
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Cell of Upholsterer-bee.}}}}
of one of certain genera of the family ''Apidæ'', such as ''Megachile'' or ''Anthocopa'', which upholsters its cell with regularly cut bits of leaves or petals of flowers. Also called ''leaf-cutter''. See ''Megachile'', ''leaf-cutter'', and ''poppy-bee''.

'''upholstering''' (up-hōl′stėr-ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''upholster'', ''v.''] '''1.''' The occupation of an upholsterer.—'''2.''' Upholstery.

'''upholstery''' (up-hōl′stėr-i), ''n.'' [< ''upholster'' + ''-y''<sup>3</sup> (see ''-ery'').] '''1.''' Furniture covered with textile material, and hangings, curtains, and the like: a general term for all such interior decorations and fittings as are made with textiles. —'''2.''' The art or trade of using textiles, leather, and the like in making furniture, decorating an interior, etc.

'''uphroe''' (ū′frō), ''n.'' [Also ''euphroe'', ''uvrou''; < D. ''juffrouw'', a young lady, also reduced ''juffer'', a young lady, in naut. use applied to “pulleys without truckles put up only for ornaments sake” (Sewel), also to spars, beams, joists, etc.:

readings.c3s1:
¶
'''upland''' (up′land), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [ME. ''upland''; < ''up'', ''prep.'', upon, on, + ''land''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''inland'', ''outland''. In the later use the ''up'' is used in its adverbial sense.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1†.''' The region in the interior; inland districts; country as distinguished from the neighborhood of towns or populous districts.—'''2.''' The higher grounds of a district; ground elevated above meadows and valleys; slopes of hills, etc.
{{smaller block|Its ''uplands'' sloping deck the mountain’s side.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Traveller.}}}}
'''3.''' ''pl.'' A grade of cotton. See ''cotton''<sup>1</sup>.

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Of or pertaining to the inland districts, or the country, as distinguished from the neighborhood of towns.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sometimes with secure delight
The ''upland'' hamlets will invite.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', L’Allegro, l. 92.}}}}
Hence—'''2†.''' Rustic; countrified; rude; savage; uncivilized. Compare ''inland'', 4. ''Chapman.''—'''3.''' Of or pertaining to uplands, or higher grounds: as, ''upland'' pasturage; also, frequenting uplands: as, the ''upland'' plover.
{{smaller block|<poem>I stood upon the ''upland'' slope, and cast
Mine eyes upon a broad and beauteous scene.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', After a Tempest.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
{{smaller|'''Upland boneset''', a tall branching thoroughwort, ''Eupatorium sessilifolium'', found from Massachusetts to Illinois and southward along the mountains.—'''Upland cotton.''' See ''cotton''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Upland flake.''' See ''flake''<sup>2</sup>.—'''Upland goose''', ''Chloëphaga magellanica'', of South America.—'''Upland Mennonite.''' See ''Mennonite''.—'''Upland moccasin''', a venomous serpent of the southern United States, related to but probably distinct from the common or water moccasin. It is not well determined, but appears to be the moccasin originally described by Troost in 1836 as ''Toxicophis atrofuscus'', by Holbrook in 1842 as ''Trigonocephalus atrofuscus'', later referred to the genus ''Ancistrodon'', and to be that commonly called ''cottonmouth''.—'''Upland plover''' or '''sandpiper''', the Bartramian sandpiper, ''Bartramia longicauda''; the uplander. See ''plover'', 3, and cut under ''Bartramia''. [New Eng.]}}

¶
'''uplander''' (up′lan-dėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' An inhabitant of the uplands.
{{smaller block|<poem>But fifty knew the shipman’s gear,
The rest were ''uplanders''.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 10.}}}}
'''2.''' The upland plover or sandpiper. [Local, Massachusetts.]

'''uplandish†''' (up′lan-dish), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uplondish''; < ''upland'' + ''-ish''.] '''1.''' Of or pertaining to uplands; pertaining to or situated in country districts: as, ''uplandish'' towns.
{{smaller block|The duke elector of Saxony came from the war of those ''uplandish'' people . . . into Wittenberg.
{{right|''Tyndale'', Ans. to Sir T. More, etc. (Parker Soc.), p. 188.}}}}
'''2.''' Hence, rustic; rude; boorish; countrified; uncultured; unrefined.
{{smaller block|The rude and ''uplandish'' ploughmen of the country are not supposed to be greatly afraid of your gentlemen’s idle serving-men.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i.}}}}
'''3.''' Upland.
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|Fifteen miles space of ''uplandish'' ground.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii.}}}}

'''uplay''' (up-lā′), ''v. t.'' To lay up; hoard. ''Donne'', Annunciation and Passion. [Rare.]

'''uplead''' (up-lēd′), ''v. t.'' To lead upward. ''Milton'', P. L., vii. 12.

'''uplean''' (up-lēn′), ''v. i.'' To lean upon anything. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|This shepheard drives, ''vpleaning'' on his batt.
{{right|''Spenser'', Virgil’s Gnat, l. 154.}}}}

'''upleap''' (up-lēp′), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''uplepen''; < ''up'' + ''leap''<sup>1</sup>.] To leap up; spring up. ''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3283. [Rare.]

'''uplift''' (up-lift′), ''v. t.'' To lift or raise up; raise; elevate: literally or figuratively: as, to ''uplift'' the arm; ''uplifted'' eyes.
{{smaller block|<poem>Earth
''Uplifts'' a general cry for guilt and wrong,
And heaven is listening.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Earth.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And shall not joy ''uplift'' me when I lead
The flocks of Christ by the still streams to feed?</poem>
{{right|''Jones Very'', Poems, p. 100.}}}}

'''uplift''' (up-lift′), ''a.'' Uplifted. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|With head ''uplift'' above the wave. ''Milton'', P. L., i. 193.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>We humbly screen
With ''uplift'' hands our foreheads.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, i.}}}}

'''uplift''' (up′lift), ''n.'' '''1.''' An upheaval. See ''upheaval.''
{{smaller block|A geologically sudden, high ''uplift'' of the northeastern part of the continent. ''Amer. Jour. Sci.'', 3d ser., XLI. 40.}}

'''2.''' Raising; elevation; mental, moral, or physical exaltation.
